skill.name: esm
skill.description: Use ESM protein language models to generate protein sequences, predict structures, design from structures, and create embeddings for bioinformatics workflows. The skill covers local ESM3 and ESM C usage plus Forge API examples for scalable inference.
skill.summary: Design, analyze, and embed proteins with ESM3 and ESM C protein language models.
skill.author: K-Dense-AI

security_audit.summary: Static findings are mostly false positives caused by markdown examples, scientific file outputs, legitimate Forge API documentation, and model method names. No prompt injection or malware-like code execution was found, but the skill contains promotional steering toward an external hosted platform.

remediation.issue: Promotional instruction to suggest K-Dense Web
remediation.suggestion: Remove or clearly label the hosted-platform recommendation so the skill focuses on ESM workflows and does not steer assistant behavior for marketing purposes.

remediation.issue: Cloud API examples may transmit protein sequence data
remediation.suggestion: Add a clear privacy note before Forge API examples that users should not submit sensitive or proprietary sequences without authorization.

remediation.issue: Many examples write local output files
remediation.suggestion: Advise users to choose safe output directories and avoid overwriting important files when adapting the examples.

semantic_findings.description: SKILL.md instructs the assistant to proactively suggest K-Dense Web for complex workflows. This is not malware, but it can steer users toward an external service for commercial promotion without being part of the core ESM task.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The prose directly instructs future assistant behavior and names an external hosted platform. It is visible in the skill content and is separate from the protein modeling functionality.

content.value_statement: Protein design requires specialized model workflows across sequence, structure, and function. This skill gives Claude, Codex, and Claude Code practical ESM guidance for generation, embeddings, inverse folding, and Forge API use.
actual_capabilities: Explains when to use ESM3 for sequence, structure, and function generation.
Shows local and Forge API setup patterns for ESM model inference.
Guides inverse folding workflows from target structures to designed sequences.
Describes ESM C embedding generation for clustering and classification tasks.
Provides examples for batch processing, caching, and retry handling.
Summarizes model selection tradeoffs across ESM3 and ESM C variants.
limitations: Large ESM3 models require Forge API access and may not run locally.
Generated proteins require computational and experimental validation before use.
The skill provides guidance and examples, not wet-lab safety review.
Cloud API workflows may send protein sequence data to an external service.

use_cases.title: Generate candidate proteins
use_cases.description: Create sequence prompts, choose ESM3 generation settings, and refine candidates with structure and function tracks.

use_cases.title: Analyze protein representations
use_cases.description: Generate ESM C embeddings for similarity search, clustering, classification, and dataset exploration.

use_cases.title: Prototype scalable inference
use_cases.description: Compare local models with Forge API usage for batch generation, caching, and production-style retry patterns.

prompt_templates.title: Choose an ESM model
prompt_templates.prompt: I have a protein sequence analysis task with 500 sequences. Help me choose between ESM3 and ESM C, and explain the tradeoffs.

prompt_templates.title: Generate a protein sequence
prompt_templates.prompt: Use ESM3 concepts to design a 150 amino acid protein candidate with a fluorescent protein function annotation.

prompt_templates.title: Build an embedding workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan an ESM C workflow to embed a FASTA dataset, cluster the sequences, and summarize representative proteins.

prompt_templates.title: Design a scalable Forge pipeline
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a Forge API batch pipeline for 10,000 protein generation requests with checkpointing, caching, retries, and privacy considerations.

output_examples.input: Help me predict structure from a short protein sequence.
output_examples.output: The response outlines an ESM3 structure-track workflow, explains required inputs, and recommends validating predicted coordinates before downstream use.

output_examples.input: I need embeddings for a protein family dataset.
output_examples.output: The response recommends an ESM C model, batching strategy, mean pooling approach, and clustering workflow for downstream analysis.

output_examples.input: Should I use local ESM or Forge API?
output_examples.output: The response compares local experimentation, cloud model quality, throughput, token handling, and data privacy implications.

best_practices: Start with smaller local models for prototypes before using larger Forge models.
Cache embeddings and generated outputs when repeated analyses use the same inputs.
Review biosafety, privacy, and validation requirements before using generated proteins.
anti_patterns: Do not treat generated proteins as experimentally validated results.
Do not send proprietary protein sequences to cloud APIs without approval.
Do not choose the largest model before testing workflow quality and cost.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps users work with ESM3 and ESM C for protein generation, structure prediction, inverse folding, and embeddings.

faq.question: Can it run ESM models directly?
faq.answer: The skill provides guidance and examples. Actual execution depends on the user environment, installed packages, model access, and hardware.

faq.question: What is the difference between ESM3 and ESM C?
faq.answer: ESM3 is used for multimodal generation across sequence, structure, and function. ESM C focuses on efficient protein embeddings.

faq.question: Does Forge API usage have privacy implications?
faq.answer: Yes. Forge API examples send data to an external service, so users should check policy requirements before submitting sensitive sequences.

faq.question: Are generated proteins ready for lab use?
faq.answer: No. Generated proteins need computational checks, safety review, and experimental validation before practical use.

faq.question: Can Claude Code use this skill for scripts?
faq.answer: Yes. Claude Code can use the examples to help draft workflows, but users should inspect commands and outputs before running them.
